challenges.name: session-keys-ttl-quiz
challenges.title: Session keys and their TTL
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from the session incident: the auth guard with a long-lived session, and a user's index set after some of their sessions disappeared.

questions.question:
The auth guard, run on every authenticated request:

const h = await this.redis.hgetall(`sess:${sid}`);
if (!h.userId) throw new UnauthorizedException();
await this.redis.expire(`sess:${sid}`, 1800);

On Monday 26 Oct 2026 at 21:00 UTC:
$ redis-cli HGET sess:9f2c createdAt
"1792828800000"          (Sat 24 Oct 2026 08:00 UTC)
$ redis-cli TTL sess:9f2c
(integer) 1794

The security policy says a session must end 12 hours after sign-in.

Statement: "With this guard, a session that sends a request at least every 30 minutes still ends 12 hours after sign-in."
questions.explanation: False. The guard resets the TTL to 1800 seconds on every request and never looks at createdAt, so the expiry slides forward forever as long as the session is used at least every 30 minutes. The evidence shows it: a session created 61 hours ago still has 1794 seconds left. To enforce the 12-hour policy, compute the seconds left until createdAt + 12 h, use the smaller of that and 1800 as the new TTL, and reject the request when nothing is left (or set an absolute expiry with EXPIREAT). The misconception is that a TTL limits the lifetime of a key; it limits the time since the last EXPIRE.

questions.question:
Sign-in adds each new session id to the user's index set. Later, on the "Your devices" page:

$ redis-cli SMEMBERS user:u_42:sessions
1) "a81f"
2) "c03d"
3) "d7e2"
4) "f19b"
5) "0b6a"
$ for s in a81f c03d d7e2 f19b 0b6a; do redis-cli EXISTS sess:$s; done
(integer) 1
(integer) 0
(integer) 0
(integer) 1
(integer) 0

Statement: "Redis kept c03d, d7e2 and 0b6a in the set although their session keys are gone, so the code that lists devices must check each session and remove the dead ids itself."
questions.explanation: True. A set member is just a string; Redis has no foreign keys and no link between the member "c03d" and the key sess:c03d. When a session key expires or is deleted with DEL alone, the set keeps the id. The application must treat the index as a hint: read each listed session (an empty HGETALL means it is gone), SREM the dead ids, and give the set itself a TTL so an abandoned index does not live forever. Deleting with DEL during sign-out-everywhere is still safe, because DEL ignores missing keys and returns how many it really removed. The misconception is that expiring a key cleans up every structure that mentions it.

challenges.name: session-keys-with-ttl
challenges.title: Session keys with sliding and absolute expiry
challenges.description: CodeDev sessions lost their TTL in a refactor and "Sign out of all devices" scanned every key. Rebuild the session store on the in-memory Redis model (FakeRedis on a FakeClock in milliseconds). A session is the hash "sess:<sessionId>" with the fields userId, device and createdAt (clock.now in ms, as a string); the set "user:<userId>:sessions" indexes the user's session ids. Write five functions. createSession(r, clock, sessionId, userId, device): return false and write nothing when sess:<sessionId> already exists; otherwise write the hash, give it a TTL of IDLE_TTL_SECONDS (1800), add the id to the index, set the index TTL to ABSOLUTE_LIFETIME_SECONDS (43200) and return true. touchSession(r, clock, sessionId), called on each authenticated request: null when the session does not exist; otherwise set the TTL to the smaller of IDLE_TTL_SECONDS and the whole seconds left until createdAt + ABSOLUTE_LIFETIME_SECONDS (rounded down); if no second is left, delete the session as deleteSession does and return null; else return the session { id, userId, device, createdAt: number }. deleteSession(r, sessionId): false when the session does not exist; otherwise delete the hash, remove the id from the user's index, return true. deleteAllSessions(r, userId): delete every session listed in the index, remove those ids from the index (an empty set disappears) and return how many sessions still existed. listSessions(r, userId): the live sessions sorted by createdAt, then id; remove ids whose hash has expired from the index; listing must not change any TTL. Input: a JSON list of steps (create, use, delete, deleteAll, list, advance, keys). The runner prints one line per step except advance; keys prints every live key with its TTL in seconds and the members of each set.
hints: For each function, ask which keys it must read, which it must write, and which TTLs it changes. Which of the five functions are allowed to change the TTL of sess:<id>, and which must leave it exactly as it was?

Look at touchSession and listSessions side by side: both read the hash, but only one is activity. In touchSession the new TTL depends on two limits - the idle TTL and the time left until createdAt + the absolute lifetime - and Math.floor of milliseconds / 1000. In listSessions, hgetall returns {} for an expired session, and srem cleans the index.

A similar rule elsewhere: a password-reset link valid for 15 minutes of inactivity but at most 1 hour after it was issued at t = 0. A click at t = 50 min gets min(900, floor((3,600,000 - 3,000,000) / 1000)) = min(900, 600) = 600 s; a click at t = 61 min finds the key gone. Looking at the reset page without clicking must not reset anything.
